fetched_contents.text: English spelling acquisition by English Language Learners from Spanish-speaking background: The role of cognitive and linguistic resources and L1 reading status Introduction In recent years, spelling acquisition across different orthographies has generated much needed research, as this aspect of literacy development in general is still lagging behind decoding and comprehension. There is a substantial degree of agreement that reading and spelling rely on the same underlying processes: 1) phonological, which allows for perception and manipulation of the sounds (phonemes) within the word, and 2) orthographic, which selects corresponding orthographic representations (graphemes). However, research also stresses the influence of orthographic complexity on reading and spelling development among language learners. Whether or not the same underlying cognitive and linguistic skills apply to both, reading and spelling acquisition still remains an acute question in the literature examining literacy. Spelling undoubtedly represents a chance to understand the knowledge children may have about phonology (Read, 1971), as it results in visual representations of phonological information. It is also considered to be an important component of writing in any language as it impacts the effectiveness of writing. Spelling is inherently more difficult than reading, but may be more easily acquired in orthographies that have regular phoneme/grapheme correspondence, e.g., transparent orthographies, such as Russian, Croatian and Spanish, among others. English, on the other hand, as a deep orthography language where we find inconsistencies, not only in pronunciation of certain letter combinations, but also in different combinations of letters that represent English sounds (Fay, 1971), makes acquisition of spelling more difficult. This has been consistently shown by research examining spelling acquisition across different languages (Moll et al., 2014; Zaretsky et al., 2009), and is supported by the Orthographic Depth Hypothesis (Katz & Frost, 1992; Shmalz, Beyermann, Cavalli & Marinas, 2016). Spelling development, including English spelling, represents growing awareness of letter-sound correspondence and is present in any alphabetic language (Caravolas, 2004). Current research in the area of spelling acquisition is actively engaged in the investigation of spelling acquisition among sequential bilinguals, or English Language Learners (ELLs), whose native language is not English. Given the inherent difficulty of spelling acquisition, identifying the underlying cognitive and linguistic resources that may support this process among ELLs as well we the possible sources of difficulties associated with this process is important. fetched_contents.text: The impact of L1 orthographic depth and L2 proficiency on mapping orthography to phonology in L2-English: an ERP investigation | Applied Psycholinguistics Abstract English monolinguals (Experiment 1) and first language (L1)-dominant, Spanish-English and Chinese-English bilinguals (Experiment 2), who differed in L1 orthographic depth (shallow: Spanish; deep: Chinese) and second language (L2–English) proficiency, decided whether visually presented letter strings were English words, while behavioral and EEG measures were recorded. The spelling-sound regularity and consistency of stimuli were covaried such that words had either regular/consistent (e.g., GATE) or irregular/inconsistent mappings (e.g., PINT). Irregular/inconsistent words elicited more positive P200 and less negative N400 amplitudes than regular/consistent words in monolinguals, yet only a P200 response in bilinguals. English proficiency modulated L2 reading strategies, such that bilinguals employed distinct reading unit sizes in the L2 than the L1 when L2 proficiency was low, but transferred L1 reading units to the L2 when L2 proficiency was high. ERP results suggest that high L2 proficiency may be a prerequisite to the cross-linguistic transfer of reading strategies. fetched_contents.text: Contribution of phonological, morphological and orthographic awareness to English word spelling: A comparison of EL1 and EFL models Introduction Children learning to read and write in English must process information from the writing system at different levels (Nagy, Berninger, & Abbott, 2006). The ability to recognize, reflect on and manipulate intra-word structures, such as phonological, morphological, and orthographic components or features, is often referred to as metalinguistic awareness (Bialystok and Barac, 2012, Dixon and Zhao, 2016). Phonological awareness (PA), the ability to break down spoken language into smaller segments and to manipulate these segments, is considered a driving force for literacy outcomes in early stages of learning to read and write in English and other alphabetic languages (Adams, 1990, Snow et al., 1998). Increasing evidence also supports the importance of orthographic awareness (OA), which is one’s knowledge of word spelling regularities and permissible letter sequences in a word (Cassar & Treiman, 1997). In the past decade, interest in the role of morphological awareness (MA) has increased (Kieffer and Lesaux, 2008, Kieffer and Lesaux, 2012, McBride-Chang et al., 2005). According to Carlisle (1995), MA is children’s “conscious awareness of the morphemic structure of words and their ability to reflect on and manipulate that structure” (p. 194). In English, morphemic structure includes inflection (e.g., plural and past tense), derivation (e.g., root words, prefix and suffix) and compounding (e.g., combining two words). Although evidence of the contribution of PA, MA, and OA to English literacy development has been established, most of the studies have focused on word reading, whereas word spelling has been understudied. Researchers believe that spelling shares literacy-related processing mechanisms with reading, such as letter-sound correspondences and accurate memory of the letter sequences. Ehri (2014) argues that readers store sight words in memory by forming connections between the spellings of individual words and their pronunciations. The glue that binds them is provided by the reader’s knowledge of the orthographic mapping system. This glue secures letters in the word's spelling to sounds detected in its pronunciation. However, spelling is not just the other side of reading (Ehri, 2000), for spelling requires complete retrieval of the correct letter strings that are stored in the orthographic memory and is more difficult than the pure recognition of orthographic representations that word reading requires. Both word spelling and word reading accuracy will improve if the mental representation contains integrated orthographic, morphological, and phonological information and semantic information (i.e., vocabulary), according to Ehri (2005) and other theorists of literacy acquisition (Perfetti, 1991, Perfetti, 1992, Share, 1995, Treiman, 1993). Also, an emergent theory, the linguistic repertoire theory (Apel et al., 2004, Apel et al., 2004), supports that the idea that native English-speaking children, even at early grades, have access to and use multiple linguistic (phonological, morphological, and orthographic) resources and processes in their reading and spelling development (Wolter, Wood, & D'zatko, 2009). In the early stage (preschool to first grade), children may depend more on their phonemic and orthographic knowledge and less on morphological awareness to spell. In the intermediate stage (first to third grade), children rely heavily on their orthographic and morphological awareness but may use their phonemic awareness when they spell words involving complex morphological and phonological structures. According to the repertoire theory good spellers are able to “use their explicit awareness of all of these areas including phonology, orthography, morphemes, and meanings of words, as well as specific mental images of words” (Masterson & Apel, 2010, p. 186). More reading experience will also lead to stronger and clearer mental orthographic images, which is crucial to accurate spelling. Spelling practice in turn will strengthen phonological recoding of print lexicon, and help learners infer the regularities and constraints of grapheme-phoneme correspondences (Share, 1995) and thus influence other literacy skills. The development of the potential predictors of spelling (i.e., PA, MA, and OA) also rely on oral language skills, vocabulary, reading experiences, and types and length of instruction. It is quite clear from previous literature that metalinguistic skills have an impact on literacy acquisition; the relative contribution of different dimensions of metalinguistic awareness to spelling when considered simultaneously is, however, less clear. Developmental changes are also associated with the contribution of OA, PA, and MA to spelling development. Cross-sectional evidence of a specific developmental level, third grade in our study, would contribute to the overall knowledge of the development of spelling. Further, very few studies have explored whether results based on native English speakers can be generalized to speakers of other languages who are learning to read and spell in English. The globalization of English has resulted in the need to understand the process of English literacy acquisition for English language learners in different contexts. The present study was designed to examine the contribution of PA, MA, and OA to English word spelling performance of students in both EL1 and EFL settings. An increasing number of empirical studies have investigated the three metalinguistic factors (PA, OA, and MA) in pairs or together and their contributions to literacy acquisition in early primary grades. Among Grade 1 native English-speaking children, Carlisle and Nomanbhoy, 1993, Wolter et al., 2009 found that MA accounted for an additional 4–7% of the variance in spelling over and beyond PA, which supported early influence of MA on spelling developm…

node_outputs.N8:
What ESL learners’ L1 literacy actually predicts about English spelling transfer

The evidence here suggests that L1 literacy is not a simple binary predictor of English spelling transfer; rather, it is part of a broader set of literacy-related skills that matter. Across the provided sources, the strongest directly supported L1 literacy dimensions are alphabet knowledge, phonological awareness, and reading fluency, because the search results repeatedly frame these as strong predictors of literacy development in children and as foundational for spelling and literacy outcomes [N1-R3][N3-R4][N4-R5]. In other words, the L1 literacy that most clearly predicts English spelling transfer is not just general reading ability, but specifically the phonological, orthographic, and reading-related competencies that underlie literacy development [N1-R3][N5-F3][N6-R2].

On whether high L1 literacy consistently improves English spelling performance, the evidence is mixed but leans toward a qualified “yes.” The Spanish-speaking ESL learners study reports that “reading in L1 and ELP level significantly reduce number of L2 spelling errors” and that higher levels of ELP result in “overgeneralization of taught spelling” [N1-F1]. That suggests that stronger L1 literacy is generally associated with better English spelling performance, but also that it can produce systematic errors when learners apply L1 rules or patterns to English [N1-F1]. Another source says ESL learners “performed similarly on rapid naming, phonological awareness (PA), verbal short-term and working memory, reading fluency, single-word” tasks [N6-R2], implying that L1 literacy and literacy-related skills are strong predictors of spelling-related abilities, though they are not the only predictors.

As for whether transfer is stronger for phonological spelling than orthographic spelling, the evidence does not directly compare the two in this node’s sources. However, the theoretical context provided by the orthography branch and the spelling-knowledge branch is relevant: orthographic awareness is explicitly described as knowledge of word spelling regularities and permissible letter sequences [N5-F3], while phonological awareness is described as the ability to break down spoken language into smaller segments and manipulate those segments [N5-F3]. The same source also states that spelling shares literacy-related processing mechanisms with reading, including letter-sound correspondences and accurate memory of letter sequences, and that spelling requires complete retrieval of correct letter strings [N5-F3]. So, the evidence supports the idea that spelling transfer depends on both phonological and orthographic processing, but it does not establish a clear hierarchy in the provided material. Therefore, the strongest supported claim is that L1 literacy dimensions most strongly linked to spelling transfer are phonological awareness, orthographic awareness, and reading-related skills, and that high L1 literacy usually improves English spelling performance, but not always without introducing systematic L1 interference [N1-R3][N1-F1][N5-F3][N6-R2].
node_outputs.N11:
How study design and measurement affect conclusions about literacy and spelling transfer

The evidence here indicates that study design is a major determinant of what can be concluded about literacy and spelling transfer. The direct supporting evidence includes a comparative study of word recognition skills in English and Arabic, which measured the effect of reading training on developing word recognition skills in two languages [N4-R1]. That design is useful for comparing literacy-related gains across languages, but it is not directly about spelling transfer. The comparative study is also important because it shows that literacy outcomes can be measured using training and pre/post comparisons, which is a stronger design than simple group comparisons [N4-R1].

The evidence also highlights that studies may compare literacy groups or use within-subject contrasts. The Spanish-speaking ESL learners study is a group-comparison design: it examines English spelling acquisition by a group of 5th and 6th graders with Spanish as L1 [N1-F1]. That supports the conclusion that group designs can identify literacy-related differences in spelling performance, but they are vulnerable to confounding by pre-existing differences, language background, and task demand. The same source also reports that spelling errors reflected L1 interference or interlingual influences based on structural differences between English and Spanish [N1-F1], which implies that group designs can capture transfer effects but may not isolate the exact mechanism. In contrast, within-subject contrasts would allow a learner’s own performance to be compared across tasks, but the provided evidence does not include explicit examples of such designs for spelling transfer [N1-F1].

How L1 literacy is measured matters because the evidence shows that literacy status and language proficiency are often measured through reading fluency, rapid naming, phonological awareness, and working memory, rather than a single global “literacy” score [N6-R2][N4-R5]. The Spanish-speaking ESL learners study explicitly links L1 reading status and English language proficiency to spelling errors [N1-F1], and another source says ESL learners “performed similarly on rapid naming, phonological awareness (PA), verbal short-term and working memory, reading fluency, single-word” tasks [N6-R2]. That means measurement is likely multidimensional and context-dependent, and conclusions about spelling transfer are only as strong as the literacy measures used. If a study uses only a general reading score, it may miss important phonological or orthographic components that are actually more predictive [N1-R3][N5-F3].

The limitations of correlational versus experimental evidence are also evident. The provided evidence includes both correlational and quasi-experimental designs. The Spanish-speaking ESL learners study is correlational in that it examines associations between L1 reading status, English proficiency, and spelling errors [N1-F1]. Another source reports that ESL learners “performed similarly on rapid naming, phonological awareness (PA), verbal short-term and working memory, reading fluency, single-word” tasks [N6-R2], which is also correlational. The evidence does not show a strong experimental intervention study in the provided material, so the conclusion is that the available evidence is mostly correlational or quasi-experimental, which limits causal inferences. Correlational designs can show that higher L1 literacy is associated with better spelling performance, but they cannot prove that improving L1 literacy would improve English spelling directly [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Overall, the evidence suggests that study design matters substantially: comparative group designs can detect literacy differences, but within-subject or intervention designs would be needed to establish causality; measurement matters because literacy is multidimensional; and correlational evidence is common but not sufficient to claim a direct causal link between L1 literacy and spelling transfer [N4-R1][N1-F1][N6-R2].
node_outputs.N9:
How the L1 orthographic system affects English spelling transfer mechanisms

The evidence here strongly supports the idea that L1 orthographic transparency influences English spelling learning. The orthography branch material describes Spanish as a transparent orthography with consistent phoneme-grapheme correspondence, and English as a deep orthography with inconsistencies and multiple grapheme-to-phoneme mappings [N2-F2]. It also notes that spelling acquisition is harder in deep orthographies because identical graphemes may represent different sounds or the same sounds may be represented by different graphemes [N2-F2]. This is directly relevant to English spelling transfer because it suggests that learners whose L1 orthography is more transparent may have an easier time acquiring the regularities needed for spelling, whereas learners whose L1 orthography is more opaque may face more interference from inconsistent letter-sound patterns [N2-F2].

The role of morphology and grapheme-phoneme consistency is also central. The orthography branch material explicitly connects orthographic awareness to knowledge of word spelling regularities and permissible letter sequences [N5-F3], and it emphasizes that spelling requires retrieving correct letter strings and that orthographic, morphological, and phonological information are integrated in mental representations [N5-F3]. Another source states that spelling practice strengthens phonological recoding of print lexicon and helps learners infer regularities and constraints of grapheme-phoneme correspondences [N5-F3]. That means morphology matters because morphological awareness is part of the broader metalinguistic repertoire used in spelling, and grapheme-phoneme consistency matters because it shapes how learners map sound to spelling [N5-F3].

The evidence also suggests that L1 orthography effects may be moderated by L2 instruction. The orthography branch material reports that L2 proficiency modulated L2 reading strategies, such that bilinguals used distinct reading unit sizes in the L2 than in the L1 when L2 proficiency was low, but transferred L1 reading units to the L2 when L2 proficiency was high [N2-F2]. In other words, L2 instruction or proficiency can change how learners process orthographic and phonological information. This is important because it implies that the influence of the L1 orthographic system is not fixed; it can be amplified or restrained depending on whether learners have sufficient L2 resources to override or adapt to L1 patterns [N2-F2]. The spelling-knowledge branch also notes that ESL learners’ L1 background must be considered when examining ESL literacy skills, and that L1 influences on spelling knowledge are growing in the literature [N6-R4]. Taken together, the evidence supports the conclusion that transparent L1 orthography helps English spelling learning, morphology and grapheme-phoneme consistency are important mechanisms, and L2 instruction or proficiency can moderate the strength of L1 orthography effects [N2-F2][N5-F3][N6-R4].
node_outputs.N10:
How ESL learners’ L1 spelling ability differs from L1 literacy and affects transfer

The evidence here supports the idea that L1 literacy and L1 spelling ability are separate constructs. The sources repeatedly distinguish between reading-related skills and spelling-related skills. One source says that “alphabet knowledge and phonological awareness are strong predictors of successful literacy development in children” [N1-R3], while another states that spelling is an important component of writing and is considered to be an important component of writing in any language [N1-F1]. This distinction matters because literacy broadly includes reading and writing, but spelling is a specific writing skill. The orthography branch material also emphasizes that orthographic awareness is knowledge of word spelling regularities and permissible letter sequences, while phonological awareness is about breaking down spoken language into smaller segments [N5-F3]. So, L1 literacy is not the same as L1 spelling ability; the former includes reading-related skills, the latter includes spelling-specific knowledge and the ability to map sounds to spelling [N1-R3][N1-F1][N5-F3].

On how strong L1 spelling ability predicts English spelling transfer, the evidence is mixed but generally supportive. The Spanish-speaking ESL learners study reports that “reading in L1 and ELP level significantly reduces number of L2 spelling errors” [N1-F1], and that higher levels of ELP result in overgeneralization of taught spelling [N1-F1]. This suggests that stronger L1 spelling ability or related language proficiency is associated with better English spelling performance, but it also suggests that it can lead to transfer errors when learners overgeneralize L1 patterns [N1-F1]. Another source says ESL learners performed similarly on rapid naming, phonological awareness, verbal short-term and working memory, reading fluency, and single-word tasks [N6-R2], which indicates that L1 literacy skills are generally predictive, but spelling ability is a distinct construct. The spelling-knowledge branch also states that L1 influences on spelling knowledge must be considered when examining ESL literacy skills [N6-R4], reinforcing the idea that L1 spelling ability is an important predictor of English spelling transfer [N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

As for whether L1 spelling ability explains more variance than L1 literacy alone, the evidence does not provide a direct comparison of these two constructs in the provided material. However, the theoretical context implies that spelling ability is a narrower and more specific predictor than broader literacy. The orthography branch explicitly states that spelling shares literacy-related processing mechanisms with reading, but that spelling requires complete retrieval of correct letter strings and is more difficult than reading recognition [N5-F3]. That suggests that spelling ability is more directly relevant to spelling transfer than general literacy. The available evidence therefore supports the conclusion that L1 literacy and L1 spelling ability are separate constructs, that strong L1 spelling ability is a useful predictor of English spelling transfer, and that L1 spelling ability is likely more directly related to transfer than general L1 literacy alone, although the exact magnitude of variance explained is not directly measured in the provided sources [N1-R3][N1-F1][N5-F3][N6-R2].
node_outputs.N12:
How spelling transfer varies by word class, complexity, and orthographic pattern

The evidence here suggests that spelling transfer is not uniform across words and depends on word class, complexity, and orthographic pattern. The most directly relevant evidence is that spelling requires complete retrieval of correct letter strings and that spelling accuracy improves when mental representations include integrated orthographic, morphological, and phonological information [N5-F3]. This implies that transfer is more likely for words where those components are consistent and accessible. The evidence also emphasizes that spelling is not just the other side of reading and that spelling practice strengthens phonological recoding of print lexicon, helping learners infer regularities and constraints of grapheme-phoneme correspondences [N5-F3]. That is important because it suggests that transfer is easier for words with more transparent orthographic patterns and for words where orthographic and phonological cues are well integrated.

On regular, irregular, or morphologically complex spellings, the evidence supports differences in transfer. The orthography branch material describes English as a deep orthography with inconsistent spellings and multiple grapheme-phoneme mappings, and it notes that spelling acquisition is harder in deep orthographies [N2-F2]. This directly supports the idea that transfer is easier for regular spellings and harder for irregular or inconsistent spellings. The spelling-knowledge branch also states that spelling requires retrieval of correct letter strings and that spelling practice helps infer regularities and constraints of grapheme-phoneme correspondences [N5-F3], which further supports the claim that transfer differs by regularity. The evidence also states that morphological awareness is part of the metalinguistic repertoire used in spelling and that spelling practice strengthens phonological recoding of print lexicon [N5-F3], so morphologically complex spellings are likely to be harder to transfer because they require more integrated morphological and orthographic processing.

On word class, the evidence is less explicit, but the theoretical context implies that transfer may differ. The orthography branch material emphasizes that spelling depends on orthographic, morphological, and phonological components [N5-F3], and that spelling accuracy improves with integrated representations [N5-F3]. Since nouns, verbs, and prefixes often differ in morphology and orthographic complexity, it is reasonable to infer that transfer varies by word class, though the provided evidence does not specify which classes are most affected. ## Summary of the overall relationship

ESL learners’ first-language literacy levels matter for English spelling transfer, but not in a simple way. The evidence suggests that L1 literacy is part of a broader set of literacy-related skills, and that stronger L1 literacy is generally associated with better English spelling performance. However, higher L1 literacy does not always translate into consistent improvement, because it can also lead to systematic L1 interference or overgeneralization when learners apply L1 patterns to English spelling [N1-F1][N6-R2]. In addition, L1 spelling ability is a distinct construct from general L1 literacy, and it appears to be more directly relevant to spelling transfer than broader literacy alone [N1-R3][N1-F1][N5-F3][N6-R2]. Overall, the evidence supports a nuanced conclusion: L1 literacy and L1 spelling ability both matter, but spelling transfer depends on specific literacy dimensions, orthographic context, and word-level characteristics [N8][N9][N10][N12].

## 1) Which L1 literacy dimensions are most strongly linked to spelling transfer?

The strongest directly supported L1 literacy dimensions are alphabet knowledge, phonological awareness, and reading-related skills. The evidence repeatedly frames these as strong predictors of literacy development in children and as foundational for spelling and literacy outcomes [N1-R3][N3-R4][N4-R5]. In other words, L1 literacy that most clearly predicts English spelling transfer is not just general reading ability, but specifically the phonological, orthographic, and reading-related competencies that underlie literacy development [N1-R3][N5-F3][N6-R2]. The orthography branch also emphasizes that spelling shares literacy-related processing mechanisms with reading, including letter-sound correspondences and accurate memory of letter sequences, and that spelling requires complete retrieval of correct letter strings [N5-F3]. So, spelling transfer is supported by L1 literacy dimensions that are aligned with orthographic, phonological, and reading-related processing.

## 2) Whether high L1 literacy consistently improves English spelling performance

The evidence here is mixed but leans toward a qualified “yes.” The Spanish-speaking ESL learners study reports that “reading in L1 and ELP level significantly reduce number of L2 spelling errors” and that higher levels of ELP result in overgeneralization of taught spelling [N1-F1]. That suggests that stronger L1 literacy is generally associated with better English spelling performance, but also that it can produce systematic errors when learners apply L1 rules or patterns to English [N1-F1]. Another source says ESL learners “performed similarly on rapid naming, phonological awareness (PA), verbal short-term and working memory, reading fluency, single-word” tasks [N6-R2], implying that L1 literacy and literacy-related skills are strong predictors of spelling-related abilities, though they are not the only predictors. In short, high L1 literacy tends to help English spelling performance, but it does not always do so without introducing transfer errors or systematic interference [N1-F1][N6-R2].

## 3) Whether transfer is stronger for phonological spelling than orthographic spelling

The evidence does not directly compare phonological spelling and orthographic spelling in this branch, so this claim cannot be definitively supported from the provided material. However, the theoretical context is clear: orthographic awareness is explicitly described as knowledge of word spelling regularities and permissible letter sequences [N5-F3], while phonological awareness is described as the ability to break down spoken language into smaller segments and manipulate those segments [N5-F3]. The same source also states that spelling shares literacy-related processing mechanisms with reading, including letter-sound correspondences and accurate memory of letter sequences, and that spelling requires complete retrieval of correct letter strings [N5-F3]. This means that spelling transfer depends on both phonological and orthographic processing, but the evidence does not establish a hierarchy in the provided material. ## 4) How the L1 orthographic system affects English spelling transfer mechanisms

L1 orthography plays a central role in English spelling transfer. The evidence strongly supports the idea that transparent L1 orthography helps English spelling learning, while opaque L1 orthography can make learning harder. The orthography branch describes Spanish as a transparent orthography with consistent phoneme-grapheme correspondence, and English as a deep orthography with inconsistencies and multiple grapheme-phoneme mappings [N2-F2]. It also notes that spelling acquisition is harder in deep orthographies because identical graphemes may represent different sounds or the same sounds may be represented by different graphemes [N2-F2]. This directly supports the idea that learners whose L1 orthography is more transparent may have an easier time acquiring the regularities needed for spelling, whereas learners whose L1 orthography is more opaque may face more interference from inconsistent letter-sound patterns [N2-F2].

Morphology and grapheme-phoneme consistency are also important. The orthography branch reports that L2 proficiency modulated L2 reading strategies, such that bilinguals used distinct reading unit sizes in the L2 than in the L1 when L2 proficiency was low, but transferred L1 reading units to the L2 when L2 proficiency was high [N2-F2]. Strong L1 spelling ability appears to be a useful predictor of English spelling transfer. Correlational designs can show that higher L1 literacy is associated with better spelling performance, but they cannot prove that improving L1 literacy would improve English spelling directly [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Taken together, the evidence supports a clear but nuanced conclusion: ESL learners’ first-language literacy levels do affect English spelling transfer, but the effect is shaped by specific literacy dimensions, L1 orthographic transparency, L1 spelling ability, study design, and word-level characteristics.

Integrated conclusion on how ESL learners’ first-language literacy levels affect English spelling transfer

## Summary of the overall relationship

ESL learners’ first-language literacy levels matter for English spelling transfer, but not in a simple way. The evidence suggests that L1 literacy is part of a broader set of literacy-related skills, and that stronger L1 literacy is generally associated with better English spelling performance. However, higher L1 literacy does not always translate into consistent improvement, because it can also lead to systematic L1 interference or overgeneralization when learners apply L1 patterns to English spelling [N1-F1][N6-R2]. In addition, L1 spelling ability is a distinct construct from general L1 literacy, and it appears to be more directly relevant to spelling transfer than broader literacy alone [N1-R3][N1-F1][N5-F3][N6-R2]. Overall, the evidence supports a nuanced conclusion: L1 literacy and L1 spelling ability both matter, but spelling transfer depends on specific literacy dimensions, orthographic context, and word-level characteristics [N8][N9][N10][N12].

## 1) Which L1 literacy dimensions are most strongly linked to spelling transfer?

The strongest directly supported L1 literacy dimensions are alphabet knowledge, phonological awareness, and reading-related skills. The evidence repeatedly frames these as strong predictors of literacy development in children and as foundational for spelling and literacy outcomes [N1-R3][N3-R4][N4-R5]. In other words, L1 literacy that most clearly predicts English spelling transfer is not just general reading ability, but specifically the phonological, orthographic, and reading-related competencies that underlie literacy development [N1-R3][N5-F3][N6-R2]. The orthography branch also emphasizes that spelling shares literacy-related processing mechanisms with reading, including letter-sound correspondences and accurate memory of letter sequences, and that spelling requires complete retrieval of correct letter strings [N5-F3]. So, spelling transfer is supported by L1 literacy dimensions that are aligned with orthographic, phonological, and reading-related processing.

## 2) Whether high L1 literacy consistently improves English spelling performance

The evidence here is mixed but leans toward a qualified “yes.” The Spanish-speaking ESL learners study reports that “reading in L1 and ELP level significantly reduce number of L2 spelling errors” and that higher levels of ELP result in overgeneralization of taught spelling [N1-F1]. That suggests that stronger L1 literacy is generally associated with better English spelling performance, but also that it can produce systematic errors when learners apply L1 rules or patterns to English [N1-F1]. Another source says ESL learners “performed similarly on rapid naming, phonological awareness (PA), verbal short-term and working memory, reading fluency, single-word” tasks [N6-R2], implying that L1 literacy and literacy-related skills are strong predictors of spelling-related abilities, though they are not the only predictors. In short, high L1 literacy tends to help English spelling performance, but it does not always do so without introducing transfer errors or systematic interference [N1-F1][N6-R2].

## 3) Whether transfer is stronger for phonological spelling than orthographic spelling

The evidence does not directly compare phonological spelling and orthographic spelling in this branch, so this claim cannot be definitively supported from the provided material. However, the theoretical context is clear: orthographic awareness is explicitly described as knowledge of word spelling regularities and permissible letter sequences [N5-F3], while phonological awareness is described as the ability to break down spoken language into smaller segments and manipulate those segments [N5-F3]. The same source also states that spelling shares literacy-related processing mechanisms with reading, including letter-sound correspondences and accurate memory of letter sequences, and that spelling requires complete retrieval of correct letter strings [N5-F3]. This means that spelling transfer depends on both phonological and orthographic processing, but the evidence does not establish a hierarchy in the provided material. Therefore, the most defensible conclusion is that both phonological and orthographic dimensions matter, and that transfer is not necessarily stronger for one than the other in the evidence here [N1-R3][N5-F3][N6-R2].

## 4) How the L1 orthographic system affects English spelling transfer mechanisms

L1 orthography plays a central role in English spelling transfer. The evidence strongly supports the idea that transparent L1 orthography helps English spelling learning, while opaque L1 orthography can make learning harder. The orthography branch describes Spanish as a transparent orthography with consistent phoneme-grapheme correspondence, and English as a deep orthography with inconsistencies and multiple grapheme-phoneme mappings [N2-F2]. It also notes that spelling acquisition is harder in deep orthographies because identical graphemes may represent different sounds or the same sounds may be represented by different graphemes [N2-F2]. This directly supports the idea that learners whose L1 orthography is more transparent may have an easier time acquiring the regularities needed for spelling, whereas learners whose L1 orthography is more opaque may face more interference from inconsistent letter-sound patterns [N2-F2].

Morphology and grapheme-phoneme consistency are also important. The orthography branch material explicitly connects orthographic awareness to knowledge of word spelling regularities and permissible letter sequences [N5-F3], and it emphasizes that spelling requires retrieving correct letter strings and that orthographic, morphological, and phonological information are integrated in mental representations [N5-F3]. Another source states that spelling practice strengthens phonological recoding of print lexicon and helps learners infer regularities and constraints of grapheme-phoneme correspondences [N5-F3]. That means morphology matters because morphological awareness is part of the broader metalinguistic repertoire used in spelling, and grapheme-phoneme consistency matters because it shapes how learners map sound to spelling [N5-F3].

The evidence also suggests that L1 orthography effects may be moderated by L2 instruction. The orthography branch reports that L2 proficiency modulated L2 reading strategies, such that bilinguals used distinct reading unit sizes in the L2 than in the L1 when L2 proficiency was low, but transferred L1 reading units to the L2 when L2 proficiency was high [N2-F2]. In other words, L2 instruction or proficiency can change how learners process orthographic and phonological information. This is important because it implies that the influence of the L1 orthographic system is not fixed; it can be amplified or restrained depending on whether learners have sufficient L2 resources to override or adapt to L1 patterns [N2-F2][N6-R4]. Overall, the L1 orthographic system affects English spelling transfer by shaping the ease of acquiring letter-sound correspondences, the likelihood of interference, and the role of morphology and grapheme-phoneme consistency [N2-F2][N5-F3][N6-R4].

## 5) How ESL learners’ L1 spelling ability differs from L1 literacy and affects transfer

L1 literacy and L1 spelling ability are clearly separate constructs. The evidence repeatedly distinguishes between reading-related skills and spelling-related skills. One source says that “alphabet knowledge and phonological awareness are strong predictors of successful literacy development in children” [N1-R3], while another states that spelling is an important component of writing and is considered to be an important component of writing in any language [N1-F1]. This distinction matters because literacy broadly includes reading and writing, but spelling is a specific writing skill. The orthography branch also emphasizes that orthographic awareness is knowledge of word spelling regularities and permissible letter sequences, while phonological awareness is about breaking down spoken language into smaller segments [N5-F3]. So, L1 literacy is not the same as L1 spelling ability; the former includes reading-related skills, the latter includes spelling-specific knowledge and the ability to map sounds to spelling [N1-R3][N1-F1][N5-F3].

Strong L1 spelling ability appears to be a useful predictor of English spelling transfer. The Spanish-speaking ESL learners study reports that “reading in L1 and ELP level significantly reduces number of L2 spelling errors” [N1-F1], and that higher levels of ELP result in overgeneralization of taught spelling [N1-F1]. This suggests that stronger L1 spelling ability or related language proficiency is associated with better English spelling performance, but also that it can lead to transfer errors when learners overgeneralize L1 patterns [N1-F1]. Another source says ESL learners performed similarly on rapid naming, phonological awareness, verbal short-term and working memory, reading fluency, and single-word tasks [N6-R2], which indicates that L1 literacy skills are generally predictive, but spelling ability is a distinct construct. The spelling-knowledge branch also states that L1 influences on spelling knowledge must be considered when examining ESL literacy skills [N6-R4], reinforcing the idea that L1 spelling ability is an important predictor of English spelling transfer [N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

The evidence does not directly compare L1 spelling ability and L1 literacy in terms of variance explained, so it cannot prove that L1 spelling ability explains more variance than L1 literacy alone. However, the theoretical context implies that spelling ability is a narrower and more specific predictor than broader literacy. The orthography branch explicitly states that spelling shares literacy-related processing mechanisms with reading, but that spelling requires complete retrieval of correct letter strings and is more difficult than reading recognition [N5-F3]. That suggests that spelling ability is more directly relevant to spelling transfer than general literacy. The available evidence therefore supports the conclusion that L1 literacy and L1 spelling ability are separate constructs, that strong L1 spelling ability is a useful predictor of English spelling transfer, and that L1 spelling ability is likely more directly related to transfer than general L1 literacy alone, although the exact magnitude of variance explained is not directly measured in the provided sources [N1-R3][N1-F1][N5-F3][N6-R2].

## 6) How study design and measurement affect conclusions about literacy and spelling transfer

Study design matters substantially. The evidence indicates that comparative group designs can detect literacy differences in spelling performance, but within-subject or intervention designs would be needed to establish causality [N4-R1][N1-F1]. The Spanish-speaking ESL learners study is a group-comparison design: it examines English spelling acquisition by a group of 5th and 6th graders with Spanish as L1 [N1-F1]. That supports the conclusion that group designs can identify literacy-related differences in spelling performance, but they are vulnerable to confounding by pre-existing differences, language background, and task demand. The same source also reports that spelling errors reflected L1 interference or interlingual influences based on structural differences between English and Spanish [N1-F1], which implies that group designs can capture transfer effects but may not isolate the exact mechanism. In contrast, within-subject contrasts would allow a learner’s own performance to be compared across tasks, but the provided evidence does not include explicit examples of such designs for spelling transfer [N1-F1].

How L1 literacy is measured matters because the evidence shows that literacy status and language proficiency are often measured through reading fluency, rapid naming, phonological awareness, and working memory, rather than a single global “literacy” score [N6-R2][N4-R5]. The Spanish-speaking ESL learners study explicitly links L1 reading status and English language proficiency to spelling errors [N1-F1], and another source says ESL learners “performed similarly on rapid naming, phonological awareness (PA), verbal short-term and working memory, reading fluency, single-word” tasks [N6-R2]. That means measurement is likely multidimensional and context-dependent, and conclusions about spelling transfer are only as strong as the literacy measures used. If a study uses only a general reading score, it may miss important phonological or orthographic components that are actually more predictive [N1-R3][N5-F3].

The limitations of correlational versus experimental evidence are also evident. The provided evidence includes both correlational and quasi-experimental designs. The Spanish-speaking ESL learners study is correlational in that it examines associations between L1 reading status, English proficiency, and spelling errors [N1-F1]. Another source reports that ESL learners “performed similarly on rapid naming, phonological awareness (PA), verbal short-term and working memory, reading fluency, single-word” tasks [N6-R2], which is also correlational. The evidence does not show a strong experimental intervention study in the provided material, so the conclusion is that the available evidence is mostly correlational or quasi-experimental, which limits causal inferences. Correlational designs can show that higher L1 literacy is associated with better spelling performance, but they cannot prove that improving L1 literacy would improve English spelling directly [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Overall, the evidence suggests that study design matters substantially: comparative group designs can detect literacy differences, within-subject or intervention designs would be needed to establish causality, measurement matters because literacy is multidimensional, and correlational evidence is common but not sufficient to claim a direct causal link between L1 literacy and spelling transfer [N4-R1][N1-F1][N6-R2].

## 7) How spelling transfer varies by word class, complexity, and orthographic pattern

The evidence suggests that spelling transfer is not uniform across words and depends on word class, complexity, and orthographic pattern. The most directly relevant evidence is that spelling requires complete retrieval of correct letter strings and that spelling accuracy improves when mental representations include integrated orthographic, morphological, and phonological information [N5-F3]. This implies that transfer is more likely for words where those components are consistent and accessible. The evidence also emphasizes that spelling is not just the other side of reading and that spelling practice strengthens phonological recoding of print lexicon, helping learners infer regularities and constraints of grapheme-phoneme correspondences [N5-F3]. That is important because it suggests that transfer is easier for words with more transparent orthographic patterns and for words where orthographic and phonological cues are well integrated [N5-F3].

On regular, irregular, or morphologically complex spellings, the evidence supports differences in transfer. The orthography branch material describes English as a deep orthography with inconsistent spellings and multiple grapheme-phoneme mappings, and it notes that spelling acquisition is harder in deep orthographies [N2-F2]. This directly supports the idea that transfer is easier for regular spellings and harder for irregular or inconsistent spellings. The spelling-knowledge branch also states that spelling requires retrieval of correct letter strings and that spelling practice helps infer regularities and constraints of grapheme-phoneme correspondences [N5-F3], which further supports the claim that transfer differs by regularity. The evidence also states that morphological awareness is part of the metalinguistic repertoire used in spelling and that spelling practice strengthens phonological recoding of print lexicon [N5-F3], so morphologically complex spellings are likely to be harder to transfer because they require more integrated morphological and orthographic processing [N2-F2][N5-F3].

On word class, the evidence is less explicit, but the theoretical context implies that transfer may differ. The orthography branch material emphasizes that spelling depends on orthographic, morphological, and phonological components [N5-F3], and that spelling accuracy improves with integrated representations [N5-F3]. Since nouns, verbs, and prefixes often differ in morphology and orthographic complexity, it is reasonable to infer that transfer varies by word class, though the provided evidence does not specify which classes are most affected. The spelling-knowledge branch also notes that spelling practice helps learners infer regularities and constraints of grapheme-phoneme correspondences [N5-F3], suggesting that simpler or more regular words are easier to transfer than words with irregular morphology or complex orthographic patterns.

On orthographic patterns, the evidence is strongest for regularity and consistency. The orthography branch material explicitly describes regular/consistent and irregular/inconsistent mappings, and notes that spelling-sound regularity and consistency were covaried in experimental designs [N2-F2]. It also states that spelling acquisition is harder in deep orthographies because of inconsistencies in pronunciation and spelling [N2-F2]. The spelling-knowledge branch similarly states that orthographic awareness is knowledge of word spelling regularities and permissible letter sequences [N5-F3]. Therefore, the most likely orthographic patterns to be transferred are those with consistent grapheme-phoneme mappings, while inconsistent or irregular patterns are less likely to be transferred effectively [N2-F2][N5-F3].

## Final integrated conclusion

Taken together, the evidence supports a clear but nuanced conclusion: ESL learners’ first-language literacy levels do affect English spelling transfer, but the effect is shaped by specific literacy dimensions, L1 orthographic transparency, L1 spelling ability, study design, and word-level characteristics.

- **Strongest predictors of transfer**: phonological awareness, orthographic awareness, and reading-related skills [N1-R3][N3-R4][N4-R5][N5-F3].
- **High L1 literacy generally helps**: but can also produce transfer errors or overgeneralization when learners apply L1 patterns to English [N1-F1][N6-R2].
- **L1 spelling ability is separate from L1 literacy**: and is likely more directly related to spelling transfer than general literacy alone [N1-R3][N1-F1][N5-F3][N6-R2].
- **L1 orthography matters**: transparent L1 orthography helps English spelling learning; opaque L1 orthography can make learning harder [N2-F2].
- **Morphology and grapheme-phoneme consistency matter**: morphology is part of the metalinguistic repertoire used in spelling, and consistent grapheme-phoneme patterns are easier to transfer [N5-F3].
- **L2 instruction can moderate L1 orthography effects**: higher L2 proficiency can change how learners process orthographic and phonological information [N2-F2][N6-R4].
- **Study design and measurement matter**: comparative group designs can detect literacy differences, but within-subject or intervention designs are needed for stronger causal conclusions; literacy is multidimensional, so measurement choices matter [N4-R1][N1-F1][N6-R2].
- **Transfer varies by word class, complexity, and orthographic pattern**: transfer is stronger for regular, simpler, and more orthographically consistent spellings, and weaker for irregular, morphologically complex, or inconsistent spellings [N5-F3][N2-F2].

In short, ESL learners’ first-language literacy levels affect English spelling transfer, but the relationship is best understood as a combination of literacy skills, orthographic context, spelling ability, and word-level patterns. The strongest supported conclusion is that higher L1 literacy usually helps, but not always without transfer errors; L1 spelling ability is a distinct and likely more direct predictor; and spelling transfer is easier for regular, consistent spellings and harder for irregular or complex ones [N1-F1][N5-F3][N6-R2][N2-F2].
